source.title: The Poincaré Conjecture 99 Years Later: A Progress Report

accepted.question_text: Does every smooth compact 3-dimensional manifold M^3 in which every simple closed curve can be deformed continuously to a point have to be homeomorphic to the 3-sphere S^3? Equivalently, is every simply connected closed 3-manifold homeomorphic to S^3?

evidence.quote:
If a smooth compact 3-dimensional manifold M 3 has the property that every sim-
ple closed curve within the manifold can be deformed continuously to a point, does
it follow that M 3 is homeomorphic to the sphere S3 ?

Since then, the hypothesis that every simply connected closed 3-manifold is homeomorphic
to the 3-sphere has been known as the Poincar¶e Conjecture.

accepted.question_text: Is every smooth homotopy 4-sphere diffeomorphic to the standard 4-sphere S^4? accepted.question_text: Which closed simply connected 4-manifolds with vanishing Kirby–Siebenmann invariant κ = 0 actually admit differentiable structures? The source identifies κ as the mod-2 Kirby–Siebenmann invariant for a topological 4-manifold and states that κ = 0 is necessary for M^4 × R to admit a differentiable structure, but that this does not settle which such 4-manifolds are themselves smoothable.

accepted.question_text: When a 4-manifold with Kirby–Siebenmann invariant κ = 0 does admit a differentiable structure, under what conditions is that differentiable structure essentially unique? The question concerns uniqueness up to inequivalent smooth structures on topological 4-manifolds in the regime discussed immediately after Freedman's classification theorem.

accepted.question_text: Does every closed 3-manifold with finite fundamental group admit a Riemannian metric of constant positive curvature, and therefore have to be homeomorphic to a spherical space form S^3/Γ for some finite subgroup Γ of SO(4) acting freely on S^3? This is Thurston's Elliptization Conjecture, and the source notes that the Poincaré Conjecture is its special case with trivial fundamental group.

accepted.question_text: Do the singularities that arise in Hamilton's Ricci flow on a closed 3-manifold with finite fundamental group always have a sufficiently special form that one can continue using the flow, after suitable analysis and rescaling, to construct a constant-curvature metric? In the source, this is the key unresolved obstacle in extending Hamilton's positive-Ricci-curvature result to the full Elliptization Conjecture.

evidence.quote:
If we start with a 3-manifold of positive Ricci curvature, Hamilton was able to carry
out this program and construct a metric of constant curvature, thus solving a very special
case of the Elliptization Conjecture. In the general case there are serious di±culties, since
this °ow may tend toward singularities. He conjectured that these singularities must have
a very special form, however, so that the method could still be used to construct a constant
curvature metric.
